The whole path, end to end

This page walks the path once, from an empty box to a product running, and says at every step: what happens, what you can press, how it can fail, and what to do about it.

One rule runs through all of it. This is a development platform, so work is not held back waiting for approval: when a run finishes, it merges, pushes, and waits for the platform to build and answer. What comes back to you is not "may I merge" but "here it is, running". Everything you decide, you decide about a product you can open.

The path in one list

  1. Write — sentences in your own words.

  2. Read — the machine reads them into subjects and claims.

  3. Keep — you keep the reading, or you do not.

  4. Group — the subjects are grouped into things worth building.

  5. Choose — you pick one, and it is worked out into promises.

  6. Build — you sign, and the run starts.

  7. The run — the door, the workers, the auditors, the closing gate.

  8. The hand-over — the work is merged and pushed.

  9. Live — the platform builds it; the address starts answering.

  10. On the running product — the promises about pages are judged there.

  11. The report — what you asked for, and what happened to each of it.

  12. The decision — it stays, or it comes back out.

The strip across the top always names where you are and the one thing to press. If you never look anywhere else, the strip is enough.

Write, read, keep

You type sentences, one per line, and press Read these N. The reading groups them into subjects and turns each into a claim, quoting your own words back. Nothing is recorded yet.

Press Keep these N and they become asks — the only thing in the store that is yours rather than derived. Everything after this can be thrown away and made again; these cannot.

If the reading is wrong — it split one sentence into two subjects, or missed one — fix the words and read again. The reading of kept asks can be redone at any time with Read again: it replaces the earlier reading whole, and nothing derived from the old one survives.

Group and choose

Group into things to build proposes sets: a few subjects that are worth building and looking at together. Proposing decides nothing.

Choose a set is what pays for working it out. Only then are its promises derived: one sentence each, where it lands in the code, and the acceptance criteria that will prove it. A documentation promise is added here when nothing else in the set lands a page.

If a set comes back empty — the machine found nothing to build from those subjects — say more about them and choose again.

Build: the signing gate

Build these N opens the cut review: every promise, every criterion, and the documentation decision. This is the last place where changing your mind is free.

Signing records what was signed, by content. If the promises change after that, the run refuses itself rather than build something you did not sign.

A criterion nothing can drive from outside the product is declared unprovable here, and rides the delivery as an observation for you rather than as a check somebody faked.

The run

The door

Before any worker starts, the run claims the repository, provisions a tree, and proves the repository’s own commands on the untouched tree — the build, the suite, the way it runs a single test. Then it places the checks a previous delivery left, and seeds the graph.

Failure What to do

the repository’s own product build fails on the untouched tree

The project does not build before this run touched anything, so nothing it delivers could ship. Fix the project first — usually the last thing merged. This is also what you see when a previous deployment failed and was never put right.

no command was proved for running a check

The repository does not say how it runs one test. Add it to thinkube.yaml or the facts file, and run again.

the signature does not match

The promises changed after signing. Sign again from the cut review.

The workers

Each slice gets its own workers, and they cannot see each other’s work: the one writing checks never sees the code, and the one writing code never sees the checks. A third brings the repository’s existing tests under the new behaviour, after the code lands.

The graph draws one card per unit, titled with the promise it keeps. Its own log is one click away. Stop aborts every live worker; the run drains and reports what it had.

Failure What to do

a unit needs you

It asked a question it cannot answer alone. Answer it in the rail; the worker carries on from your words.

a unit failed

Its own note says why. The run goes on with the rest and the gate reports the promise as undelivered. Run it again repairs from what is there.

the run goes silent

It says so itself, names what has not moved, and stops rather than sit there. Run it again.

The auditors and the closing gate

Every slice is graded against its own criteria, on the real state. Then the closing gate judges the whole delivery: the repository’s suite on the delivered tree — or, where no suite runs locally, the repository’s own product build — every assessment read by a fresh reviewer, then the finisher and, last, the closer.

The closer repairs what is failing and nothing else. Anything it changes that no failure named is reported to you on the delivery.

Failure What to do

the suite or the build is red and stays red

The delivery is withheld: nothing is merged. The report names what failed. Run it again is the one press.

a check could not run at all

That is the machine’s failure, not the work’s. It is reported as unjudged and never counted against a promise.

The hand-over

The record is written, the work is committed, merged into the project and pushed. The branch goes with the merge: a repair starts from the project, not from a branch of history.

Failure What to do

the merge conflicts with your checkout

Named in git’s own words, with the files. Commit or stash what is in the way, then run again. Nothing was changed.

merged, but the push was refused

The work is in the project; the platform never saw it. Push it yourself when the remote is reachable.

Live

The run waits, and says what it is waiting on: the platform noticing the push, then the build step by step, then the address answering. The deployment is a node in the graph like any other, because everything judged on the running product waits for it.

If the platform refuses the build, the run repairs what the platform’s own words name — only those files — proves the repository’s build passes locally, and pushes again. Twice. Then it stops and gives the answer back to you.

Failure What to do

the platform will not build it

The card says so in the platform’s words, and that until the project builds, nothing else can be built here. Three presses: Ask Claude to fix it opens a session in that repository with the platform’s words and what was already tried; Ask the platform again re-reads the build, which is what you press after a fix; Roll it back takes the work out of the project.

the address never answered

The platform built it, but the app did not come up. Look at the app’s own logs; the work is in the project and the build is green.

this repository is not deployed by the platform

Nothing is waiting for. The delivery is judged on its checks alone.

On the running product

A promise about a page cannot be settled by reading code. Once the address answers, one reviewer per criterion opens the product in a browser and does what the criterion describes.

Which criteria those are is read from the repository: the route with the shortest path names the container that answers at the address, and a promise landing in that container’s directory is a promise about the page. What is read rather than driven — an assessment — and what is settled elsewhere stay where they are.

Each reviewer is held to three limits: no repository is opened to it, it carries only the address, and the browser refuses every other origin. A reviewer that never answers leaves the criterion unjudged — never a pass nobody saw.

The report

The report answers, sentence by sentence, what you asked for and what happened to it. Under it: what the machine could not judge, what only you can certify, the promises answered after the merge, and the run’s own account for a developer.

Button What it does

Keep it

The work is already in the project. This closes the decision, retires the run’s number, and lets the promises stand as built. It moves nothing in git.

Accept it

The same press for a delivery that was never merged — an older one, or a repository the platform does not deploy. Here it does merge and push.

Roll it back

Reverts this delivery’s merges and every delivery this space merged after it, newest first, and pushes. The project builds as it did before. Refused, with the commit named, if somebody else’s commit sits on top — taking this out would take that with it.

Not this

The same press for a delivery that was never merged: the work stays on its branch, and the signed promises can run again.

Run it again

Runs the signed promises again, from the project as it stands.

Ask Claude to fix it

Opens a Claude session in that repository, with the promises, the address, the platform’s own words and what the run already tried.

Ask the platform again

Re-reads what the platform did with the merged work. Press it after a fix: a card frozen at a failed build stops saying so.

It held / It did not

For a promise only a person can settle — installed on a clean machine, seen working. Your word closes it.

Say it does not hold

For a promise that is in the project and does not do what you asked. Available at any time, on any cut, however old. It puts that promise back on the board, and the ordinary Build repairs it.

When something is wrong later

Nothing about a delivery is final. Work that is live and wrong is said to be wrong on the promise itself — Say it does not hold, in your own words — and that promise becomes work again. This is the same act for a cut from an hour ago and a cut from last month, and it is the honest one: the product is what it does, not what its checks said on the day.

Two things that stay true

A run leaves the project buildable, or it says exactly how it did not. The door proves the build before anything starts, the gate proves it before anything merges, and the live phase repairs what the platform refuses. When it cannot, it says so in the platform’s words and hands you the presses that change something.

What cannot be proven is never claimed. An unjudged check is unjudged, an unreachable reviewer is unreachable, and a criterion nobody could drive is yours to certify. A green that nobody earned is the one thing this machine will not print.
